title: Designing Observation and Action Models for Efficient Reinforcement Learning with LLMs
claim: Our method reaches near-peak performance several times faster than the standard baseline while matching its final asymptotic performance.
layout: single line plot, return vs timesteps, dashed vertical lines mark convergence points
description: A single learning-curve plot titled 'Basic Locomotions (stand, walk, run)'. The x-axis is timesteps in millions (0–10) and the y-axis is return (0–~950). A blue line with circle markers and a light blue confidence band, labeled 'Ours (LOAM)', rises sharply to about 900 by roughly 2.5M steps and then plateaus. A gray line with triangle markers and a gray band, labeled 'FastTD3', rises much later and only approaches the plateau near 9M steps. Two vertical dashed lines, one blue at about 3M and one gray at about 8.8M, mark where each method converges. This makes the roughly 3× speedup visible. A legend sits at the bottom right. The eye goes first to the steep blue curve and the gap between the two dashed lines.
caption: LOAM is 3× faster than default benchmark model (FastTD3) across HumanoidBench stand, walk, and run tasks.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for semantic reasoning, enabling the formalization of tasks that traditionally relied on manual human intuition. This capability extends to environment design in reinforcement learning. While prior research predominantly focuses on reward design, the design of observation and action spaces remains relatively underexplored. We propose LLM-based design of Observation and Action Models (LOAM), a framework leveraging LLMs to construct refined agent spaces from raw environments. To mitigate the computational burden of identifying the best candidate model from stochastic LLM outputs, LOAM incorporates a continuous racing mechanism that dynamically allocates resources to prioritize the most promising configurations without additional training overhead. Empirical evaluations on HumanoidBench and Isaac Lab demonstrate that LOAM consistently outperforms handcrafted baselines in both learning speed and asymptotic performance.
